title: Standing waves
examples: What is the relationship between the length of a string and its fundamental frequency?
How do nodes and antinodes help us understand wave patterns?
Can you explain the difference between the fundamental frequency and the second harmonic?

explain.say: Today we explore standing waves and their patterns.
A node is a point where the wave always has zero movement.
An antinode is the place of maximum vibration for the wave.
The fundamental frequency is the lowest possible frequency of vibration.
Higher harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.
When you pluck a string, the fundamental frequency is the first harmonic.

faq.q: What is the difference between the fundamental frequency and the first harmonic?
faq.a: They are the same thing. The fundamental frequency is the name for the lowest frequency, and the first harmonic is the first integer multiple of that frequency.
asks: Is the fundamental the same as n=1?

faq.q: Do standing waves only happen on strings?
faq.a: No, standing waves can occur in pipes, air columns, and even on vibrating membranes. The principle remains the same.
asks: Can sound waves make standing patterns?
Where else do I see standing waves?

faq.q: How do I calculate the frequency of the third harmonic?
faq.a: You multiply the fundamental frequency by three. The formula is simply n times the fundamental frequency, where n is three.
asks: If n is three, what is the frequency?
What is 3 times the basic frequency?

faq.q: Are nodes always points of zero amplitude?
faq.a: Yes, by definition, a node is a point on the wave where the displacement, or the amplitude, is zero at all times.
asks: Does the wave ever move at a node?
Is zero displacement the definition of a node?

faq.q: Does the length of the string affect the harmonics?
faq.a: Yes, the length of the string determines the spacing between the nodes and antinodes, which in turn affects the frequencies of all harmonics.
asks: Does a longer string change the harmonics?
How is string length related to frequency?

facts: Nodes are points of minimum displacement on a standing wave.
Antinodes are points of maximum displacement on a standing wave.
The fundamental frequency corresponds to the first harmonic (n=1).
Harmonics occur at integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

quiz.say: If the fundamental frequency of a pipe is 200 hertz, what is the frequency of the third harmonic?
quiz.why: The third harmonic is three times the fundamental frequency, so 3 times 200 hertz equals 600 hertz.

wrong.0: This is the second harmonic, not the third.
wrong.1: This is half the fundamental frequency, which is incorrect.
wrong.2: This is the fundamental frequency itself, not the third harmonic.

quiz.say: Where is the displacement zero on a standing wave?
quiz.why: Nodes are specifically defined as points where the wave always has zero movement.

wrong.0: The midpoint can be a node or an antinode depending on the wave.
wrong.1: Equilibrium is a general term, but 'node' is the specific physics term.
wrong.3: Antinodes are points of maximum vibration, not zero.

quiz.say: A vibrating string has a fundamental frequency of 50 hertz. What is the frequency of the second harmonic?
quiz.why: The second harmonic is two times the fundamental frequency, so 2 times 50 hertz equals 100 hertz.

wrong.0: This is the fundamental frequency, not the second harmonic.
wrong.1: This is half the fundamental frequency, which is incorrect.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes the third harmonic when the second is asked.
